summary: Maximise (min element of a subarray) x (sum of the subarray) over all subarrays; return it modulo 1e9+7.
mainInsight: Fix each element as the minimum of its subarray; the best subarray for that minimum extends until a strictly smaller element on each side. Prefix sums give the range sum, and a monotonic stack gives the boundaries - then take the maximum before applying the modulus.

approaches.summary: For each i find the left/right nearest smaller; score = nums[i] * range_sum.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal; the modulus is correctly applied only at the end.

promptVariants: Why is it enough to consider each element as the subarray minimum with the widest range?
Why take the maximum before applying the modulus?
cards.answer: For a fixed minimum value all values are non-negative, so a wider subarray has a larger sum: the widest range (up to the nearest strictly smaller element on each side) is optimal for that minimum. The modulus would break comparisons, so compare real (big-int) values and reduce only at the end.
keyPoints: Widest range for a fixed min
Compare exact values; mod at the end
cards.explanation: Python's big integers make this safe.
Prefix sums, two monotonic-stack passes and a final scan are all linear.

for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    while stackL and nums[stackL[-1]] > nums[i]:
        idx = stackL.pop()
        boundL[idx] = i + 1
    stackL.append(i)

best = max(nums[i] * (prefix[boundR[i] + 1] - prefix[boundL[i]]), best)
cards.answer: Scanning right-to-left, an element popped by a strictly smaller nums[i] has its left boundary just after i (the nearest smaller to its left). The mirrored pass gives the right boundary. Strict `>` lets equal elements extend each other's ranges, which is right because equal minima do not reduce the minimum. The prefix difference is the sum of the range [boundL, boundR].
